extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and readers interested in the history and practice of journalism (especially colonial/American press)
extracted.subtask_description: A book-chapter account of the colonial American press describing how newspapers and printers assumed political power and shaped public opinion in the run-up to the Revolution. Emphasizes practices, tactics, and social roles of 18th-century journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boldness of the press
rubrics_metrics.description: The press developed a boldness that made its practitioners leaders in the revolutionary movement and a primary factor in the struggle against authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: James Franklin, Zenger, Bradfords; boldness earned respect and following and allowed printers to influence political action. Anti-pattern: timid or purely deferential reporting that fails to challenge authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberty of the press as a foundational idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Freedom of the press was one of the most firmly rooted ideas in the colonies and foundational to public life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat freedom of the press as core value that enables other democratic rights (habeas corpus, trial by jury, representation). The text treats this as a precondition for the press's political role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press as instrument for arousing the people
rubrics_metrics.description: The press functioned as the instrument by which the people were aroused to oppose oppression and to question authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guiding purpose: stimulate popular indignation and cohesive action (e.g., to break down Tory defenses). Anti-pattern: press that merely reports without mobilizing when mobilization is the goal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the press explicitly for political purposes/propaganda
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspapers were deliberately used as organs of political clubs and movements (e.g., Samuel Adams and the Independent Advertiser) to promote causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Independent Advertiser begun from a political club; Whig Club papers. Producing a paper as a political instrument is an accepted and common practice in this period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declared freedom from factional private designs
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers may declare themselves 'of no party' and commit to being 'free to Truth, Good Manners and good Sense' while avoiding licentious reflections, insolence and abuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example wording from Independent Advertiser. This is a public-facing pledge of fairness/self-restraint; guidance: such declarations can coexist with political aims but set standards for tone and decorum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open to all parties but influenced by none
rubrics_metrics.description: A paper may state that it is 'open to all parties, but influenced by none', promising inclusiveness while retaining editorial independence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Isaiah Thomas's Massachusetts Spy used this wording. Practical implication: accept contributions from diverse viewpoints but avoid being a mouthpiece for outside patrons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match style to audience: common sense in common language
rubrics_metrics.description: To influence the laboring classes, journalism must employ common sense and plain language, as learning and elegance are needed for the more cultivated classes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thomas's statement: tailor diction and style to the intended class/audience. Anti-pattern: using overly scholarly language when trying to reach common people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vehemence and passion as necessary mobilizing tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Vehemence (strong, passionate argument) was often necessary to arouse and stir the people, despite criticism from more cautious observers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Thomas's vehement rhetoric attracted criticism but was judged necessary for mobilization. Balance required between inflaming and informing; but mobilizing contexts may call for stronger rhetoric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical/production superiority vs price and reach
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical quality and ambitious production (size, paper format, imported materials) can give a paper mechanical superiority, but such superiority does not guarantee wider circulation or lower price.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Boston Chronicle printed on a whole sheet quarto with superior materials yet sold at same price as other papers; such investment may indicate official backing or a prestige strategy. Consider cost, audience, and subsidization when evaluating production choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subsidized press and governmental backing
rubrics_metrics.description: A newspaper may be subsidized by government as a means for authority to use the press to defend its cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Boston Chronicle was 'unquestionably subsidized by the British Government.' Practical implication: check for patronage/subsidy as a sign of partiality and official influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neutrality often collapses into partisanship
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers that begin with claims of neutrality frequently shift to openly espouse one side when political necessity dictates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Boston Chronicle initially appeared impartial but later espoused the Loyalist cause. Use as a caution: declared neutrality is not always durable under political pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of symbolic devices and rallying imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers used visual devices, emblems, mottos and even numbers as rallying cries or propaganda (e.g., Franklin's serpent 'Join or Die', '45', 'Illustrious 92').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: symbols and repeated motifs can unify and mobilize readers; anti-pattern: weak or inconsistent symbolism that fails to convey clear identity or cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution tactics to reach broader or working-class audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: Tactics such as free distribution, increased frequency (three issues a week) and tailoring content help obtain subscriptions from mechanics and other time-limited workers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the Massachusetts Spy scattered its first number free and planned thrice-weekly issues to attract working-class readers. Consider distribution and pricing strategies to expand audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printers' legal and personal courage
rubrics_metrics.description: Printers' willingness to litigate, resist prosecution, suffer imprisonment, or sue for damages demonstrated the printer's role in asserting press rights and in shaping public impression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Daniel Fowle's suit for damages after arrest; printers punished (paper burned, threats). Practically, assess an editor's commitment to press freedom by their responses to repression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Papers as explicit organs of party identity
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspapers frequently served as official or semi-official organs for political factions (Whig, Tory, Patriot), shaping and reflecting partisan identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Boston Gazette and Massachusetts Spy for Whigs; News-Letter and Chronicle for Loyalists; Holt's Journal as organ of Liberty. Evaluate editorial lineup and contributor lists to determine partisan alignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press's role in nation-building and the formation of public ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals left traces of nascent national ideas and helped develop conceptions of a free and independent nation through commentary and prophecy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: consider press as a formative arena for national ideology (e.g., articles forecasting America's greatness); the press both reflects and shapes emerging national identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organization through clubs and literary societies
rubrics_metrics.description: Political clubs and societies used newspapers to coordinate action, disseminate arguments, and recruit contributors (e.g., Whig Club papers and Independent Reflector).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical implication: look for networked production (clubs, contributors) as a sign of organized political press activity rather than purely commercial enterprise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of reprisals and mob action against perceived enemies
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists and printers faced mob violence, effigies, parades of soldiers, burning in effigy, and forced flight when their papers antagonized powerful interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Thomas threatened with tarring and feathering; papers burned; publishers forced to relocate. Evaluation of journalistic courage must account for physical danger endured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience segmentation: appeal to laboring classes vs cultivated readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Different papers targeted different social strata — some aimed at 'plain people' (laboring classes) with simple language, others appealed to 'cultivated' readers with scholarly contributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Thomas aimed at laboring class; Edes and Gill appealed to more cultivated writers. Guidance: align content, tone, and distribution with intended demographic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credibility through careful compilation and reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Reputation for being 'the best compiler of news' or industrious, scrupulous reporting contributed to a paper's authority and influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Richard Draper earned reputation as best compiler of news. Guidance: accuracy, collection diligence, and reputation-building practices increase trust and long-term influence.
